analysis.one_liner: Makes pharmacy benefit managers legally responsible to health plans as fiduciaries and requires them to disclose their compensation.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan pair of House members introduced the bill on December 18, 2025, and it was sent to the Education and Workforce Committee, where it awaits action.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are the middlemen that decide which drugs are covered by employer health plans, negotiate rebates from drug makers, and process prescription claims. This bill changes federal benefits law so PBMs are treated as fiduciaries — meaning they would be legally required to act in the health plan's best interest, not their own. It also requires PBMs to disclose all the money they make from a plan, and bars contracts that let them off the hook if they breach that duty.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with employer-sponsored health insurance, and the employers who sponsor those plans, would gain leverage over PBMs. Fiduciary status gives plan sponsors a legal cause of action when a PBM steers the plan toward drugs that pay the PBM more, and the disclosure rules would expose hidden compensation — spread pricing, rebate tricks, and fees — that drives up what plans and patients pay.

how_it_helps.text: Deems any company that builds a plan's drug network or formulary, negotiates rebates, processes claims, or performs utilization review to be an ERISA fiduciary, legally obligated to serve the plan's interest [S2].
Requires PBMs and third-party administrators to disclose all direct and indirect compensation they expect to receive from a plan, including money from drug manufacturers and rebate aggregators [S2].
Bars indemnification — no contract can relieve a PBM of liability for breaching its fiduciary duty, and any such contract is void as against public policy [S2].

Prevents a covered service provider (like a PBM) from serving as the 'responsible plan fiduciary' overseeing the disclosure process itself, closing a self-policing loophole — except for a PBM's own employee plan [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The three dominant PBMs — which process the large majority of employer prescription drug claims and profit from rebates, spread pricing, and opaque fees — would bear new legal liability and lose revenue from arrangements a fiduciary duty would not permit. Health insurers that own PBMs would share that exposure. Some compliance and litigation costs could eventually be passed to plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant PBMs and insurers that own them

drawbacks.text: Fiduciary status exposes PBMs to ERISA lawsuits, and compliance costs for disclosures could be significant; smaller third-party administrators might exit the market for small employer plans, reducing options [S2].

The bill changes PBMs' legal duties but does not directly cap drug prices or restructure the rebate system, so manufacturers and PBMs could adapt their pricing in ways that preserve much of the status quo.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half of Americans with employer coverage, the potential upside is real: fiduciary duty and forced disclosure strike at the core of how PBMs make money at plans' expense. The costs — new litigation and compliance burdens — fall mostly on the industry being regulated, though some could trickle down to plans. The main limitation is that the bill works through liability and transparency rather than direct price controls, so its impact depends on how aggressively fiduciary standards are enforced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has not received a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) introduced the bill on December 18, 2025, joined by Rep. Mackenzie as the sole cosponsor, giving it one Democrat and one Republican [S1, S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which holds jurisdiction over ERISA; no further action has been taken [S4].
The bill would amend ERISA to deem PBMs fiduciaries for group health plans, require detailed compensation disclosures, and prohibit contracts indemnifying PBMs for fiduciary breaches [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: dominant PBMs keep operating without fiduciary duties while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Rep. Jake Auchincloss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make PBMs fiduciaries under ERISA and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two sponsors are one Democrat and one Republican; no one has yet opposed it on the record, and no committee or floor action has occurred.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: These companies profit from rebate negotiation, spread pricing, and opaque fees on employer drug plans. Fiduciary status and forced compensation disclosure would directly expose and constrain those revenue streams, and ending indemnification removes their contractual shield from lawsuits. The three biggest PBMs process most employer prescription claims, so the burden lands on a small, concentrated industry.

Most major insurers own the largest PBMs, so fiduciary liability and disclosure requirements reach their integrated pharmacy businesses. Costs to these firms could ultimately show up in plan premiums, but the bill's purpose is to stop practices that overcharge plans today.

Manufacturers pay the rebates PBMs negotiate and could face pressure on the rebate system's structure. Some could benefit if fiduciary standards reduce PBM steering toward high-rebate drugs, though the bill leaves the rebate system itself intact.

Plan sponsors get a legal duty owed to them and required disclosure of what their PBMs are paid, strengthening their hand in negotiations. They may take on some oversight responsibilities for the disclosures.

analysis.trajectory: This is a two-week-old bill with one cosponsor and no committee activity. Most bills introduced in the House never get a hearing, let alone a vote, and the odds here are low. That said, PBM regulation is one of the few issues with active bipartisan interest in this Congress, so a companion effort or a broader PBM package could absorb these provisions; on its own, it is likely to stall in committee unless the Education and Workforce chair schedules a markup.
